metaDescription: Six 110W foldable solar panels compared on bifacial versus N-type cells, station cable kits, folded size and weight for topping up a power station.
expertTake: The ZOUPW 110W N-type panel is the best overall because its cable kit and cell quality suit most stations. The EASYLONGER ESP110 is the value pick for anyone already owning that maker's stations. If you want to refill a large battery in a day, skip this class and buy a 200W or bigger panel.
introParagraphs: A panel around a hundred watts is the working partner of a mid-size power station. It is too big to slip into a jacket and too small to recover a large battery quickly, so it occupies the useful middle where weekend campers and van users live.

Because the size is similar across brands, the real separation comes from the cells under the surface, the cable kit in the box, the weight you carry from the car and how well the folds survive repeated setup. Efficiency claims are everywhere and decide almost nothing.

products.name: ZOUPW 110W N-Type 16BB Foldable Panel with Multi-Plug Cable
products.description:
The cells here are N-type with sixteen busbars, a construction that spreads current across more conductors so a hairline crack or a shaded patch costs less output. N-type silicon also ages slowly and shrugs off heat better than older P-type cells, which shows up on a hot campsite afternoon. The surface is ETFE laminate rated IP67.

What tips it to the top slot is the cable. Instead of the common four-in-one lead that fits a handful of stations, ZOUPW supplies a cable with five distinct connector options, aimed at the Jackery and EcoFlow style inputs that account for much of the market. Buying a panel and then hunting for a matching plug is the most common frustration with this class, and this one removes it.

The panel folds like a briefcase, so treat the handle as a load point and do not hang gear from it. Inspect the connector heads every season for bent pins, and wipe grime off the cell surface with a damp cloth. If you see a bright spot or a discolored strip across a cell, that is delamination starting and the panel deserves a close look.
products.bestFor: Campers who own a mainstream power station and want matching plugs in the box.
pros: N-type 16BB cells hold up under heat and small cracks
Cable offers five connector options for common stations
ETFE surface with IP67 rating
Strong all-round build for the class
cons: Folded size is briefcase-big for a daypack
Cell efficiency claim is cell-level, not panel-level

products.name: ZOUPW 110W Bifacial N-Type Foldable Panel, 6.83 lb
products.description:
A bifacial panel collects light on both sides, with the rear catching what bounces off the ground. Over pale gravel, sand or snow that rear contribution is real, though over dark grass it is small. This ZOUPW version pairs bifacial design with N-type 16BB cells and a proprietary composite surface that the maker says out-transmits standard ETFE.

At 6.83 lb it is lighter than the TPDEFZQ, which weighs 8.15 lb with its controller attached, and it sits near the MHPOWOS at about 7.5 lb. The rear cells need an unobstructed back, so the panel earns its keep when you prop it on its kickstands over reflective ground instead of laying it on a mat. Anyone camping on forest floor or a tent tarp will see little gain.

Because both faces are active, treat the back as seriously as the front. Do not lay it face down on dirt, and wipe the rear if you set it on wet ground. A composite surface is newer than ETFE, so check the finish for scuffing after a season and keep it away from sharp rock when folding.
products.bestFor: Campers on light-colored ground who want extra harvest from reflected light.
pros: Bifacial design adds output over reflective ground
N-type 16BB cells on both faces
6.83 lb is lighter than several rivals in the class
Composite surface aimed at higher light transmission
cons: Rear gain is small over grass or dark ground
Composite surface has a shorter field record than ETFE

products.name: MHPOWOS 110W Foldable Panel, 20V Output, IP67
products.description:
MHPOWOS offers the straightforward version: monocrystalline cells at a 25.5 percent claim, a 20V output and a solar extension cable that connects to its own multi-plug cable. The panel weighs 3.4 kg and folds to roughly 22.83 x 21.65 x 1.57 inches, a flat square sheet that slips behind a car seat or into a van cabinet.

It is the budget-minded option in this comparison, and the savings come from a less elaborate cable set and a plainer construction than the ZOUPW N-type. The extension cable is a useful extra, since a short factory lead often forces the station into the sun. Expect solid but unremarkable output on a clear day, with the 20V rating matching the input window of many mid-size stations.

Check the output voltage against your station before you buy, because a 20V open-circuit figure sits near the upper limit for a few small inputs. Wipe the cells with a damp cloth, store the panel flat with the cable coiled loosely, and do not leave it in a hot vehicle, where adhesive softening is the quiet killer of laminated panels.
products.bestFor: Budget buyers who want a clean, simple 110W panel with an extension cable.
pros: Extension cable lets you keep the station in shade
20V output suits many mid-size station inputs
Flat folded shape stores easily behind a seat
IP67 rated laminate
cons: Plainer cables and cells than the N-type ZOUPW
Weighs about 7.5 lb, heavy for hiking

products.name: SolarEpic 110W Bifacial Panel with Angle Guide and Kickstand
products.description:
SolarEpic is the only panel here with a printed angle guide, and a kickstand bracket that adjusts across a 40 to 50 degree range. Most people prop a panel at whatever angle the stand falls, and the guide gives a concrete target for typical latitudes, which is worth more than a point of cell efficiency. The bifacial rear is claimed to add up to 15 percent in the right conditions.

The open-circuit voltage is listed at 25.9V, an unusual number worth reading carefully. Many stations accept up to 28V, and a few small inputs cap at 22V, so check your station's maximum before connecting. In cold weather, voltage rises, so the headroom narrows on a crisp morning. This is the detail that decides compatibility far more than wattage.

Because the rear is active, keep the stand footing clean and avoid setting the panel on dark tarp. The adjustable bracket is a mechanical part that loosens over time, so check the pivot screw at the start of each trip. Rinse sand from the hinges, which otherwise wears the fabric seams around the folds.
products.bestFor: Careful setups where precise tilt and bifacial gain are worth the effort.
pros: Printed angle guide and a 40 to 50 degree adjustable stand
Bifacial design claims up to 15 percent extra
25.9V Voc is clearly published
Monocrystalline cells on both faces
cons: 25.9V Voc exceeds a few small station input limits
Adjustable bracket is a wear part

products.name: TPDEFZQ 110W N-Type Panel with Controller and USB Ports
products.description:
This panel arrives with a controller attached, offering two USB-A ports and a third multifunction port, so it can charge phones directly and drive a battery without a separate regulator. N-type cells sit under an ETFE surface rated IP67. For campers who do not own a station but want to trickle a 12V battery and charge a phone, the controller makes it a self-contained kit.

It is also the heaviest panel in the lineup at 8.15 lb, and it folds to 20.27 x 22.99 x 1.37 inches. That is a meaningful carry from the car, and the weight comes mostly from the controller housing and the frame. The ports let it work as both a station feeder and a phone charger, but the controller is the part to protect from moisture and heat.

Because the controller sits on the panel, avoid dropping the panel on that corner and keep the housing out of puddles. Inspect the ports and wiring after each trip. If the panel will live in a vehicle, shade the controller side, since electronics left in a hot cabin age faster than silicon cells ever will.
products.bestFor: Users with a bare battery who need a controller and USB ports in one unit.
pros: Controller with three output ports is built in
N-type cells with ETFE and IP67 rating
Charges phones and 12V batteries directly
Slim 1.37 inch folded thickness
cons: Controller housing is a weak point in rain or heat

products.name: EASYLONGER ESP110 110W Panel, XT60, Anderson, DC, USB
products.description:
EASYLONGER designs the ESP110 around its own ES960, ES720 and ES400 AIR stations, so the connector set of XT60, Anderson and DC and the voltage window were chosen to match. That is the main reason to buy it: if you own one of those stations, the panel is the lowest-risk way to charge it, with a stated 23.4 percent cell efficiency as a secondary point.

The USB-C and USB-A ports on the panel itself let you charge small devices without bringing the station into the picture, a small convenience that the plain panels lack. It sits at the lowest rung of the lineup for cost, trading the N-type cells and bifacial design of the others for a simple, workable build.

Outside the maker's ecosystem it is less compelling, since the matching advantage disappears and the cells are conventional. If you do own a compatible station, check the connector locking on the Anderson end each season, because a loose Anderson plug is a quiet source of lost charging. Fold along the seams, keep the panel dry and store it flat.
products.bestFor: Owners of the maker's ES-series stations who want a matched panel.
pros: XT60, Anderson and DC connectors match the maker's stations
USB-C and USB-A ports built into the panel
Lowest rung of cost in the lineup
Simple build with no unusual electronics
cons: Conventional cells with no N-type or bifacial advantage
Matching benefit applies only to that maker's stations

buyingCriteria.explanation: A panel that cannot plug into your station is useless regardless of its efficiency. The ZOUPW N-type ships a five-option cable and the EASYLONGER lists XT60, Anderson and DC. Look up your station's solar input connector and voltage window first.

Voc rises as temperature falls, so a panel listed at 25.9V, like the SolarEpic, may read higher on a cold morning. If your station caps input near 28V, that margin matters. Always compare Voc, not wattage, to the input limit.

Bifacial panels like the SolarEpic and ZOUPW bifacial gain from reflected light over pale ground, while N-type cells hold output in heat and age slowly. On sand or snow bifacial pays off; on a hot gravel lot N-type does. Choose by where you camp.
The ZOUPW bifacial weighs 6.83 lb, the MHPOWOS about 7.5 lb and the TPDEFZQ 8.15 lb. All fold to roughly a briefcase. If you carry it more than a few steps, ounces add up.

A controller on the panel, as on the TPDEFZQ, suits bare 12V batteries. A station already has one, so the extra electronics are dead weight and an extra failure point. Pick it only if you have no station.

A 110W label gives about 66 to 88 watts in strong sun, so over a day it adds roughly 350 to 450 watt-hours. That refills a 300Wh station about once on a clear day, but a 1,000Wh unit will take two or three days.

specDecoder.meaning: Sixteen busbars per cell spread current across more conductors. That reduces losses from cracks and shading.
specDecoder.watchFor: The ZOUPW panels list 16BB, while the others do not publish busbar count.

specDecoder.meaning: Active cells on both faces collect direct light from the front and reflected light from the rear. Gains vary from nearly zero over dark ground to 15 percent over bright ground.
specDecoder.watchFor: The SolarEpic claims up to 15 percent extra; treat that as a best case.

specDecoder.meaning: Open-circuit voltage is the highest the panel reaches with no load. A station's input limit must sit above it, with margin for cold.
specDecoder.watchFor: The SolarEpic is the only panel listing Voc clearly.

specDecoder.meaning: Dust-tight and immersion-rated at the panel body. It does not protect open connectors or a controller housing.
specDecoder.watchFor: The TPDEFZQ's controller is the part exposed in wet weather.

specDecoder.meaning: Two common DC connectors for stations. Anderson is bulky and robust, XT60 is smaller and common on EcoFlow-style units.
specDecoder.watchFor: The EASYLONGER lists both, along with DC.

howWeEvaluated.title: Wattage class filter
howWeEvaluated.description: Only panels rated at 110W stayed. We dropped 100W and 120W panels and kit panels with controllers sold as different classes, so the lineup shares one size and one job.

howWeEvaluated.title: Station compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared connector sets and voltage claims, from the ZOUPW's five-option cable to the EASYLONGER's XT60 and Anderson set. We also noted the SolarEpic's published 25.9V Voc.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cell and surface technology
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared N-type, bifacial and standard monocrystalline cells with ETFE or composite surfaces. Efficiency numbers were treated as cell-level.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and fold
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared weights from 6.83 lb on the ZOUPW bifacial to 8.15 lb on the TPDEFZQ, along with folded sizes and thickness.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at repeated complaints about connector fit, stand durability and exaggerated claims. Repeated complaints of that kind pushed a panel down the ranking.

rows: Feeding a Jackery or EcoFlow type station
Camping on sand, snow or gravel

cards.label: Bifacial panels
cards.text: The SolarEpic and ZOUPW bifacial add output from the rear over reflective ground. They need a stand that lets light reach the back, and the gain is small over grass.

cards.label: N-type panels
cards.text: The ZOUPW N-type and TPDEFZQ resist heat losses and age slowly. They give steady output on any ground, with no dependence on reflection.

howToChoose.note: Pick bifacial for sand and snow, N-type for hot or mixed ground.

howToChoose.subheading: Bare Panel vs Panel with Controller

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A connector set that matches your station, a Voc below its input limit with cold margin and a weight you can carry from the car. Seven pounds is manageable, and eight is where people start leaving it home.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The ZOUPW 110W N-type is the safest fit for mainstream stations, and the ZOUPW bifacial at 6.83 lb is a lighter alternative if you camp over bright ground.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You use it every weekend or in hot weather. The ZOUPW 110W N-type and the SolarEpic 110W add better cells and a stronger setup.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You charge a station a few times a year. The EASYLONGER ESP110 or MHPOWOS 110W does the job for less.

maintenance.why: A bent pin or a loose Anderson plug cuts charging quietly. The EASYLONGER and ZOUPW cables both have several heads to check.

maintenance.task: Wipe both faces of bifacial panels
maintenance.why: The rear is active on the SolarEpic and ZOUPW bifacial, so dirt there costs output.
The SolarEpic's adjustable bracket loosens with use. A loose pivot sags the panel off its target angle.
The TPDEFZQ's electronics sit on the panel. Keep them dry and out of a hot vehicle.
Heat softens laminate adhesives and a folded panel pressed under gear can crack cells.

faq.q: How much does a 110W panel add in a day?
faq.a: In good sun about 66 to 88 watts for several hours, so roughly 350 to 450 watt-hours. That refills a 300Wh station once, but a larger station needs several days.

faq.q: Is bifacial worth the extra cost?
faq.a: Over sand, snow or light gravel it can add a noticeable share from the rear. Over grass or dark ground the gain is small, so it depends on where you camp.

faq.q: Will it fit any power station?
faq.a: Only if the connector and voltage window match. Check the station's solar input specification, and use the panel's multi-plug cable or an adapter where needed.
A station's solar input has a maximum voltage. Panels produce higher voltage in cold weather, so a panel near the limit can exceed it on a cold morning and fail to charge or damage the input.

faq.q: Do I need a separate controller?
faq.a: Not for a station with built-in solar input. A bare battery needs one, and the TPDEFZQ includes it. Match any controller to the battery chemistry.
Choose 110W for a lighter carry and a mid-size station. Choose 200W if you want a faster refill or a larger battery, accepting more weight.
